documents.title: ISBI International Society for Burn Injuries practice guidelines for burn care

chunks.content: Introduction Cervical scar contracture is a common complication following burn injuries in the neck region. In addition to causing cosmetic deformities, severe cervical scar contracture often leads to functional impairments, such as incomplete mouth closure and limited neck mobility, which can significantly impact the patient’s physical and psychological well-being [ ]. In pediatric patients, the consequences of scar contracture may progressively worsen as the child grows, further compromising function. Currently, for cervical scar contractures that impair function, surgical treatments such as Z-plasty or flap reconstruction are commonly recommended [ – ]. However, in addition to the invasive nature of surgery and the airway risks associated with cervical procedures, postoperative complications such as flap necrosis, poor wound healing, and recurrence of contracture occur at a relatively high incidence. Therefore, finding effective non-surgical treatment alternatives is of significant importance [ ]. Since 2013, the Department of Burn and Plastic Surgery at our hospital has developed a Custom-Made Cervical Orthosis specifically tailored for pediatric patients with cervical scar contracture. Clinical applications have shown promising results, with this orthosis offering a viable alternative to surgical interventions in certain cases. The present study introduces the treatment method using custom-made cervical orthoses and analyzes its efficacy in a series of cases. Materials and methods Patients The present study utilized a self-controlled design. Due to ethical considerations, no parallel control group was established. A total of 11 pediatric patients admitted to the Department of Burns and Plastic Surgery at Quhua Hospital of Zhejiang from June 2019 to June 2024 were included in this study and underwent treatment with a Custom-Made Cervical Orthosis. The specific inclusion criteria were as follows: Age < 18 years; Presence of severe cervical scar contractures secondary to burn injury; No prior surgical treatment to the neck, including skin grafting or scar revision; Received custom-made cervical orthosis therapy > 6 months. Preparation of the cervical orthosis and treatment method The preparation of the cervical orthosis followed these steps: First, the patient’s neck circumference and neck length were measured. Cotton pads were then cut to appropriate sizes based on these measurements. Typically, the length of the cotton pad was about 5 cm shorter than the patient’s neck circumference, while the thickness of the pad was adjusted according to the neck length. The cotton pad was rolled tightly in a towel-like manner and then wrapped diagonally with large gauze (Fig. a). During treatment with the custom-made cervical orthosis, the patient was positioned in a seated posture with the head tilted backward or lying flat with the head tilted backward. The prepared neck brace was then placed around the neck and gently tightened by the patient’s hands to ensure a snug fit. A knot was tied at the back of the neck, with the tension adjusted so that one finger could fit comfortably between the orthosis and the neck, ensuring the patient could tolerate it. The chin was typically kept parallel to the ground or slightly elevated, and the orthosis should not extend beyond the chin to prevent excessive looseness, which would undermine the effectiveness of the pressure (Fig. b). Typically, when the patient’s neck scar is in the proliferative phase, the cervical orthosis needs to be worn continuously for 24 h a day. While during the scar atrophic phase, it can be adjusted to be worn during the day, with relaxation at night. Its size and tightness should be continuously adjusted based on changes in the patient’s neck extension. Other rehabilitation measures In addition to the custom-made cervical orthosis, all patients received a comprehensive and standardized rehabilitation program. Topical anti-scar medications were routinely applied to the cervical region, including silicone gel (Scar-ban) or compound heparin sodium and allantoin gel (Contractubex) [ , ]. Based on specific clinical indications and the preferences of the patients or their legal guardians, a subset of patients also underwent fractional laser therapy targeted at the cervical scars. Considering the significant risks of systemic side effects in the pediatric population—most notably the suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and potential growth retardation, as well as local complications like skin atrophy—none of the patients received intralesional corticosteroid injections [ ]. Furthermore, for burn injuries involving other anatomical sites, general rehabilitation interventions were implemented. These measures included the application of topical medications, pressure therapy, functional stretching exercises, and Activities of Daily Living (ADL)-oriented functional training, aiming to prevent further scar contracture and facilitate the overall functional recovery of the patients post-injury [ ]. Data collection Patient demographic data and injury details were collected. To evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of the custom-made cervical orthosis, measurements of the cervicomental angle (CMA) and cervical range of motion (ROM) were performed before and after treatment. To ensure maximal consistency, all clinical measurements were performed by the same senior rehabilitation physician. For each parameter, three consecutive measurements were taken using

measures included the application of topical medications, pressure therapy, functional stretching exercises, and Activities of Daily Living (ADL)-oriented functional training, aiming to prevent further scar contracture and facilitate the overall functional recovery of the patients post-injury [ ]. Data collection Patient demographic data and injury details were collected. To evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of the custom-made cervical orthosis, measurements of the cervicomental angle (CMA) and cervical range of motion (ROM) were performed before and after treatment. To ensure maximal consistency, all clinical measurements were performed by the same senior rehabilitation physician. For each parameter, three consecutive measurements were taken using a standard goniometer and clinical photography, with the average value recorded for analysis to minimize random measurement error. The physician followed standardized anatomical landmarks for all assessments to ensure longitudinal reproducibility. CMA was defined as the angle formed by the line connecting the mandibular angle to the hyoid bone and the line from the hyoid bone to the suprasternal notch (upper border of the sternum) [ ]. Cervical ROM covered five specific directions—extension, left lateral flexion, right lateral flexion, left rotation, and right rotation. For extension measurement, the goniometer axis was placed over the external auditory meatus with the stationary arm perpendicular to the floor and the moving arm aligned with the base of the nares; for lateral flexion, the axis was placed over the C7 spinous process with the stationary arm kept vertical to prevent shoulder compensation and the moving arm aligned with the external occipital protuberance; and for rotation, the examiner took a superior view from the cranial vertex, placing the axis over the center of the vertex while the stationary arm was held parallel to the bi-acromial line and the moving arm was aligned with the tip of the nose [ , ]. The clinical symptoms related to cervical contracture caused by the patients before and after the treatment were also recorded. At discharge, patient satisfaction was assessed via the 24-item Inpatient Satisfaction Questionnaire (IPSQ). Items were rated from 1 (very dissatisfied) to 5 (very satisfied), yielding a total score out of 120 [ , ]. Additionally, during the final follow-up, the long-term quality of cervical scars was evaluated using the Patient and Observer Scar Assessment Scale (POSAS), which consists of two parts: the Observer Scar Assessment Scale (OSAS) and the Patient Scar Assessment Scale (PSAS). Under this assessment framework, the patient and a trained observer independently scored various parameters of the scar, including itching, pain, color, stiffness, thickness, and regularity, with lower scores indicating scar conditions closer to normal skin [ ]. Detailed contents of the IPSQ and POSAS scales are provided in Appendix 1. Statistical analysis The normality of the data was tested using the Shapiro-Wilk test. For normally distributed data, values were expressed as mean ± SD, and significant differences before and after treatment were assessed using paired t-tests. For non-normally distributed continuous variables, data were expressed as median (25th percentile − 75th percentile), and significant differences were evaluated using paired samples Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Categorical variables were expressed as number (percentage) and compared using the Fisher exact test. To further quantify the clinical magnitude of therapeutic efficacy, both percentage change and effect sizes were calculated. The percentage change for continuous variables was derived based on the group means using the formula: [(Mean post - Mean pre ) /Mean pre ]×100%. To ensure robust estimation given the small sample size, 95% confidence intervals (CI) for the percentage change were generated using a bootstrapping method with 10,000 resamples. Effect sizes were determined using Cohen’s d for paired samples (d z ), defined as the mean difference divided by the standard deviation of the difference. Effect sizes were interpreted according to Cohen’s conventional guidelines: 0.2 (small), 0.5 (medium), and 0.8 (large) [ ]. For categorical clinical symptoms, percentage change was calculated as the relative reduction in incidence. Additionally, to evaluate potential confounding effects, a subgroup analysis was conducted to compare improvement magnitudes and assessment scores between patients who received adjunctive fractional laser therapy and those who did not. Group comparisons were performed using the independent samples t-test for normally distributed variables and the Mann-Whitney U test for non-normally distributed variables. A p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All statistical analyses were performed using R software version 4.2.2. The mean total body surface area (TBSA) affected by burns was 16 ± 11% TBSA, while the median area of third-degree burns was 4 (IQR, 2–8) % TBSA. Results Demographic and clinical characteristics of the pediatric patients Among the 11 pediatric patients who underwent treatment with the custom-made cervical orthosis, 8 (72.7%) were male and 3 (27.3%) were female. The median age of all patients was 2 (interquartile range [IQR], 1–3) years. The mean total body surface area (TBSA) affected by burns was 16 ± 11% TBSA, while the median area of third-degree burns was 4 (IQR, 2–8) % TBSA. The cervical burn wounds of all patients healed via secondary intention (spontaneous healing). At a median of 1 (IQR, 0–3) month following wound healing, patients initiated treatment with the custom-made cervical orthosis and continued for more than six months, with a mean treatment duration of 13 ± 5 (range 6–24) months. Regarding adjunctive therapies, all patients utilized standard topical medications, including Silicone Gel (Scar-ban, n = 10) or Compound Heparin Sodium and Allantoin Gel (Contractubex, n = 1), and 4 patients (36.4%) received between 1 and 4 sessions of fractional laser therapy during their follow-up, while the remaining 7 (63.6%) patients did not receive any fractional laser therapy to the neck (Table ). Appendix 2 further documents detailed individual baseline characteristics and treatment specifics. Data are shown as the median (25th percentile, 75th percentile), mean±standard deviation or the number of patients (%), as appropriate. Time Post-injury: Duration from the initial burn injury to the start of orthosis treatment; Time Post-healing: Duration from wound closure to the start of orthosis treatment. Comparison of cervical scar contracture before and after custom-made cervical orthosis Neck scar contracture-related variables before and after treatment are summarized in Table ; Fig. . Following treatment, the CMA significantly decreased from a median of 140° (IQR: 130°–155°) before treatment to 120° (IQR: 115°–120°) after treatment ( p < 0.001), representing a 16.6% reduction (95% CI: -20.5% to -12.2%) with a large effect size (Cohen’s d = 1.84, 95% CI: 0.87 to 2.81). The cervical ROM showed significant improvements in all five directions ( p < 0.001). Notably, cervical extension increased by 183.7% (95% CI: 119.0% to 317.2%; Cohen’s d = 3.92, 95% CI: 2.18 to 5.66), and rotation improved by over 165%. Additionally, the incidence of clinical symptoms associated with cervical scar contracture decreased significantly after treatment. All patients exhibited complete resolution of inability to close the mouth, facial organ displacement and forced head flexion. The prevalence of lower lip eversion was reduced to only one patient after treatment. Patient satisfaction and scar follow-up results The evaluation of treatment satisfaction at discharge resulted in a mean IPSQ score of 106.55 ± 5.92, indicating high guardian satisfaction with the custom-made cervical orthosis. All patients completed a follow-up period of more than two years without any surgical intervention for the neck. At the final follow-up, the median POSAS score for long-term scar quality was 19 (IQR: 14–21), suggesting that the cervical scars had achieved satisfactory aesthetic and functional maturation. Subgroup analysis of adjunctive fractional laser therapy To evaluate the potential confounding effect of adjunctive CO2 fractional laser therapy, a subgroup analysis was performed comparing patients who received laser treatment ( n = 4) with those who did not ( n = 7). The results are summarized in Table . There were no significant differences between the two subgroups in the improvement of CMA ( p = 0.285) or in most cervical ROM parameters, including lateral flexion and rotation (all p > 0.05). Notably, the laser group demonstrated a significantly greater improvement in cervical extension compared to the non-laser group (median: 45.0° [IQR, 43.8–46.2] vs. 30.0° [IQR, 27.5–35.0], p = 0.013; Cohen’s d = 2.39, 95%CI 0.81 to 3.97). Regarding patient-reported and clinical assessments, no significant differences were observed between the subgroups in either the IPSQ scores at discharge ( p = 0.152) or the POSAS scores at the final follow-up ( p = 1.000). Case presentation Case 1 involves a 1-year-old male infant who sustained scald burns covering 15% TBSA, involving the face, neck, anterior chest, and extremities. Hypertrophic scarring developed in the cervical region during the healing process. Complete wound healing was achieved approximately two months post-injury, and the patient was admitted to our hospital three months later due to severe scar contracture and associated deformities. Pre-treatment assessment revealed significant restriction in the cervical ROM: flexion 30°, extension 0°, left lateral flexion 10°, right lateral flexion 10°, left rotation 10°, and right rotation 10°. Clinically, the patient presented with lower lip eversion, incompetence of oral closure, displacement of facial features, and a forward head posture. Following admission, the patient underwent an 8-month course of treatment with a custom-made cervical orthosis. Adjunctive therapies included the daily application of topical silicone gel (Scar-ban) and three sessions of fractional laser therapy (at approximately 1, 3, and 5

hospital three months later due to severe scar contracture and associated deformities. Pre-treatment assessment revealed significant restriction in the cervical ROM: flexion 30°, extension 0°, left lateral flexion 10°, right lateral flexion 10°, left rotation 10°, and right rotation 10°. Clinically, the patient presented with lower lip eversion, incompetence of oral closure, displacement of facial features, and a forward head posture. Following admission, the patient underwent an 8-month course of treatment with a custom-made cervical orthosis. Adjunctive therapies included the daily application of topical silicone gel (Scar-ban) and three sessions of fractional laser therapy (at approximately 1, 3, and 5 months post-admission). After 8 months of intervention, the hypertrophic scarring was markedly reduced. Cervical ROM improved significantly to: flexion 50°, extension 45°, left lateral flexion 45°, right lateral flexion 40°, left rotation 65°, and right rotation 60°. The CMA decreased from 175° to 135°, and all pre-existing clinical symptoms were effectively resolved. At the 2-year post-treatment follow-up, the patient exhibited no significant clinical symptoms in the cervical region, and the remaining scars did not interfere with his ADL. The follow-up POSAS score for the neck was 34, and the IPSQ score was 110. The treatment timeline and representative clinical photographs are presented in Fig. . Case 2 involves a 3-year-old male patient who sustained alcohol flame burns covering 42% TBSA, involving the head, face, neck, trunk, and upper extremities, with 25% TBSA being III-Degree burns. Wounds achieved complete healing approximately two months post-injury, and the patient was admitted to our center for rehabilitation one month later. At admission, the patient exhibited significant hypertrophic scarring in the cervical region with a baseline CMA of 150°. Pre-treatment cervical ROM was: flexion 50°, extension 40°, left lateral flexion 45°, right lateral flexion 45°, left rotation 60°, and right rotation 60°. Clinical presentation included lower lip ectropion, incompetence of oral closure, and a forced forward-flexed head posture.Treatment for the cervical region consisted of a custom-made cervical orthosis and daily application of topical silicone gel (Scar-ban); notably, no fractional laser therapy was administered to the neck scars during the treatment period. For burn injuries at other anatomical sites, general rehabilitation interventions were implemented, including several sessions of fractional laser therapy on the face and chest. Following 24 months of continuous orthosis therapy, the CMA improved to 120°, and cervical ROM significantly increased to: flexion 50°, extension 60°, left lateral flexion 45°, right lateral flexion 45°, left rotation 80°, and right rotation 80°. Approximately one year into the treatment, the patient developed prominent keloids on the bilateral ears and left shoulder due to his keloid diathesis. These were subsequently managed via scar excision and suturing at an external facility (ears) and scar release at our hospital (upper limbs and left shoulder). At the 4-year follow-up, the cervical region—which had received no surgical intervention—showed stable scar maturation with no significant clinical symptoms or functional limitations in ADL. The follow-up cervical POSAS score was 21, and the IPSQ score was 108. The treatment timeline and representative clinical photographs are presented in Fig. . Discussion In recent years, as advancements in acute burn care have improved survival rates, the management of post-burn scar contractures has become a paramount challenge [ ]. Cervical contracture is one of the most common and severe sequelae, leading to impairments in movement, breathing, speech, and nutrition, as well as aesthetic disfigurement. This problem is particularly pronounced in pediatric patients, who face a unique set of physiological challenges distinct from adults [ ]. The primary contribution of this study is the demonstration that a non-invasive, custom-made orthosis can effectively manage severe contractures in this vulnerable demographic, filling a critical clinical gap for toddlers and young children for whom early surgical intervention carries high risks of recurrence and perioperative complications. Treating neck contractures in young children requires a fundamental departure from adult protocols, primarily due to the mechanism of “growth antagonism.” Unlike the static anatomy of adults, the pediatric cervical spine and mandible undergo rapid elongation. In the presence of rigid hypertrophic scarring, this somatic growth creates a dynamic tension where the skeletal frame lengthens while the pathological scar tissue remains static. This antagonism generates a continuous flexion moment that can progressively worsen the deformity, potentially leading to irreversible secondary skeletal complications such as micrognathia, dental malocclusion, and cervical kyphosis [ , ]. While surgical release is the standard for mature contractures, its application in growing children is often complicated by “growth-induced recurrence,” necessitating repeated procedures to keep pace with skeletal development [ , , ]. Our non-surgical orthotic approach offers a strategic advantage by managing these contractures dynamically during growth. By providing continuous mechanical counter-tension, this method potentially spares young children from the compounding physiological and psychological trauma of invasive procedures, including the potential systemic risks associated with repeated general anesthesia and surgical stress [

leading to irreversible secondary skeletal complications such as micrognathia, dental malocclusion, and cervical kyphosis [ , ]. While surgical release is the standard for mature contractures, its application in growing children is often complicated by “growth-induced recurrence,” necessitating repeated procedures to keep pace with skeletal development [ , , ]. Our non-surgical orthotic approach offers a strategic advantage by managing these contractures dynamically during growth. By providing continuous mechanical counter-tension, this method potentially spares young children from the compounding physiological and psychological trauma of invasive procedures, including the potential systemic risks associated with repeated general anesthesia and surgical stress [ – ]. Ultimately, the early and consistent implementation of orthotic therapy allows for the optimization of functional outcomes while ensuring that the treatment remains in harmony with the child’s ongoing physical development. Continuous pressure therapy acts as a cornerstone in pediatric scar management, functioning through mechanotransduction to modulate the fibroproliferative response. By applying sustained mechanical loading, pressure devices create local hypoxia and downregulate mechanosensitive pathways, thereby inhibiting myofibroblast differentiation and promoting orderly collagen realignment [ , ]. This intervention is uniquely advantageous in children, whose active somatic growth and high collagen turnover rates endow their tissue with superior biological plasticity compared to adults. Consequently, early mechanical intervention can effectively steer the immature pediatric scar toward a normotrophic phenotype before irreversible fibrosis establishes [ – ]. The use of orthotic devices is one of the most effective methods for delivering continuous pressure therapy to cervical scars [ ]. However, it has been observed that conventional plastic orthoses are often too rigid, preventing a snug fit around the neck and offering inadequate pressure distribution; specifically, they fail to conform to the complex concave-convex curves of a child’s neck, leading to uneven pressure application. Some cervical braces, designed for general surgical use, employ soft inner foam for enhanced comfort; however, they fail to provide sufficient pressure to manage the contracture effectively [ ]. Our custom-made cervical orthosis was designed to overcome these limitations, offering several key advantages especially relevant to pediatric care. First, the snug fit of our orthosis ensures optimal pressure distribution via “stress shielding,” effectively converting the mechanical tension of growth into a remodeling force. Second, the design of the orthosis incorporates cotton padding and large gauze, which not only provides sufficient rigidity to maintain the functional position of the neck but also allows for slight movement, reducing tension caused by limited neck rotation. This dynamic conformity is critical for pediatric compliance, as it accommodates swallowing and spontaneous head rotation without generating the shear forces that cause pain in active toddlers. Third, the orthosis is easy to apply and replace, with a simple manufacturing process. Given the rapid somatic growth of children, this adjustability ensures the device can “grow with the child,” avoiding the frequent and costly replacements required by rigid custom molds. Fourth, because pediatric skin is thinner and more fragile, scars are prone to blistering and ulceration during recovery. The breathable cotton and gauze construction helps prevent maceration and infection by protecting the area. Additionally, the innermost layer of the orthosis can be used in combination with silicone gel sheets or other scar management products, further enhancing its effectiveness in preventing and treating scar formation. Collectively, these structural and functional refinements allow the device to overcome the pitfalls of conventional orthotic devices, offering a cost-effective and highly adaptable strategy tailored to the unique developmental demands of growing children. In this self-controlled case series, patients treated with the custom orthosis achieved significant improvements in both the CMA and cervical ROM. While direct comparisons with surgical literature must be approached with caution due to heterogeneity in patient age and scar maturity, our functional outcomes align with the improvements reported in surgical series [ , ]. For example, in a report by Geneviève et al. [ ], a total of nine patients, including children and adults, with cervical contracture were treated surgically. Preoperative average neck mobility in five directions (Extension, Left lateral flexion, Right lateral flexion, Left rotation, Right rotation) was 24°, 19°, 24°, 46°, and 40°, respectively; after free flap surgery, mobility improved to 47°, 34°, 33°, 66°, and 69°, respectively. In our series of 11 pediatric patients, the pre-treatment average neck mobility in the five directions was 20°, 24°, 24°, 28°, and 29°, respectively; post-treatment, it improved to 56°, 43°, 43°, 74°, and 74°, respectively. Zhang et al. [ ] highlighted the functional and aesthetic importance of the CMA and, through surgical treatment, successfully reshaped the CMA to 90–120° in 50 severe cervical burn contracture cases. In comparison, our non-surgical treatment reduced the CMA from a median of 140°to 120°. Crucially, our study observed a significant resolution of clinical symptoms, including the inability to close the mouth and facial distortion. [ ] highlighted the functional and aesthetic importance of the CMA and, through surgical treatment, successfully reshaped the CMA to 90–120° in 50 severe cervical burn contracture cases. In comparison, our non-surgical treatment reduced the CMA from a median of 140°to 120°. Crucially, our study observed a significant resolution of clinical symptoms, including the inability to close the mouth and facial distortion. These improvements are reflected in the high satisfaction scores reported by parents (IPSQ), as parents valued the ability to correct functional and aesthetic deformities while sparing their children from the risks of surgery. Furthermore, our long-term follow-up results showed a median POSAS score of 19 (IQR: 14–21), which is categorized as mild scar severity. This indicates that the neck scars of pediatric patients treated with custom-made orthoses have successfully matured with a minimal aesthetic burden [ , ]. Collectively, these findings highlight that our custom-made cervical orthoses serve as a cost-effective and high-compliance strategy, effectively leveraging physiological remodeling mechanisms to avoid the necessity of surgical intervention. Notably, in this study, a subset of patients received adjunctive CO2 fractional laser therapy, which warrants careful consideration. Our subgroup analysis revealed that while the laser group achieved a significantly greater improvement in cervical extension, no significant differences were observed in CMA correction, other ROM parameters, or treatment satisfaction (IPSQ) and scar maturation (POSAS) outcomes. These findings suggest that adjunctive laser therapy may act synergistically with the orthosis to achieve superior functional outcomes, likely by enhancing scar elasticity through collagen remodeling [ ]. However, it is crucial to emphasize that patients in the non-laser group also achieved substantial and clinically meaningful improvements across all functional and structural domains, including a median extension increase of 30.0°. This indicates that while multimodal management is beneficial, the custom-made cervical orthosis remains the fundamental driver of contracture resolution. Additionally, it is important to acknowledge that the observed improvements likely result from a synergistic effect of the orthosis intervention and the natural maturation process inherent to pediatric scars. As all patients in our study initiated treatment within 6 months post-injury—corresponding to the active proliferative phase of scar formation—the orthosis was uniquely positioned to guide this vigorous biological remodeling into a functional anatomical alignment. This mechanical guidance effectively counteracted the retractive forces of the maturing scar, preventing the contracture that would typically occur if the tissue were left to heal without direction. Drawing upon our clinical experience in managing pediatric patients with neck scar contracture, we proposed a clinical decision algorithm to guide therapeutic strategy selection (Fig. ). Beyond the quantitative clinical results, we share two typical cases that successfully regained cervical mobility and symptom relief through custom-made cervical orthosis, thereby avoiding the necessity of surgical intervention. These cases also highlight the value of multimodal management: Case 1 exemplifies the efficacy of combining orthoses with fractional CO 2 laser to expedite the softening of active scars [ ]. Case 2 reveals that even for patients with a keloid diathesis—manifested by keloids on the ears and shoulders—the continuous pressure provided by the orthosis remains a potent strategy for inhibiting cervical contracture [ ]. Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First and most critically, our results are constrained by the inherent limitations of a self-controlled case series design, which restricts causal inference. The absence of a concurrent comparator group—such as a cohort receiving standard pressure therapy alone or undergoing observation only—makes it difficult to definitively isolate the therapeutic efficacy of the orthosis from the natural maturation of pediatric hypertrophic scars. Given that such scars can undergo significant spontaneous remodeling over 24–36 months, the lack of a formal temporal control analysis makes it challenging to quantify the specific contribution of the orthotic intervention beyond this biological progression [ ]. Second, the small sample size ( n = 11) restricts the statistical power and the generalizability of our findings. Third, the potential for selection bias cannot be excluded, as successful long-term orthotic treatment depends heavily on high treatment compliance from both patients and their guardians, which may not fully represent the broader pediatric population with neck scar contractures. Fourth, although CMA and ROM measurements were standardized and performed by a single senior evaluator, the lack of inter-rater or intra-rater reliability analysis leaves a potential risk of measurement bias. However, the observed improvements in CMA and ROM in our cohort substantially exceeded the 5° to 10° error margin typically associated with clinical goniometry [ , ]. This suggest that the changes are more likely to represent clinically meaningful progress than simple measurement variability. Finally, patient- or caregiver-reported outcome measures, such as the POSAS, were not implemented at the early stages of the study,

However, the observed improvements in CMA and ROM in our cohort substantially exceeded the 5° to 10° error margin typically associated with clinical goniometry [ , ]. This suggest that the changes are more likely to represent clinically meaningful progress than simple measurement variability. Finally, patient- or caregiver-reported outcome measures, such as the POSAS, were not implemented at the early stages of the study, leading to a relatively one-dimensional assessment of initial scar severity. Future multi-center prospective studies with larger cohorts and extended follow-up are warranted to validate these findings and to evaluate the long-term efficacy of this therapy, as well as its synergistic effects with other interventions. Conclusion Custom-made cervical orthoses provide significant anatomical and functional benefits for pediatric patients with post-burn cervical scar contractures. This non-surgical treatment effectively reduces the CMA, enhances neck mobility, and alleviates related clinical symptoms. Furthermore, the therapy yields high patient satisfaction; long-term follow-up exceeding two years demonstrated that the scars maintained a “mild scar severity” level. These findings underscore the clinical potential of this therapy, which may obviate the need for subsequent reconstructive surgery in a substantial proportion of pediatric patients. documents.title: ISBI Practice Guidelines for Burn Care Part 2

chunks.content: 1. Introduction Hospitalization in itself constitutes a negative experience [ ]. When afflicted by illness, patients not only endure physical suffering caused by the disease but also experience psychological and emotional stress responses such as tension, pressure, frustration, and sadness triggered by the state of being unwell [ ]. Even adults may fall into varying degrees of anxiety. For children whose mental and cognitive functions are still developing, the distress brought by hospitalization is even more intense [ ]. When hospitalized due to illness, children must leave familiar environments such as home and school to enter an unfamiliar setting. They constantly perceive the tension of their primary caregivers while enduring the pain and discomfort caused by medical procedures such as repeated blood draws and scheduled intravenous infusions, further exacerbating their fear and anxiety [ ]. During hospitalization, peripheral venous catheterization is an essential procedure and the most widely used method for establishing vascular access [ ]. Compared to single, brief venipunctures, the catheterization process is more complex and time-consuming, inevitably prolonging the child’s anticipation of pain and experience of discomfort. International studies indicate that 50% to 60% of children report significant pain and anxiety during venous puncture, with nearly 63.0% subsequently developing “needle phobia” [ , , ], which can lead to childhood phobias, pre-treatment anxiety, and treatment resistance [ ]. Distraction techniques refer to a coping strategy that involves guiding an individual’s attention toward non-painful stimuli, thereby temporarily shifting their focus away from distressing experiences such as pain or anxiety [ ]. This approach has been demonstrated to effectively minimize children’s fear, anxiety, and perception of acute pain associated with venous access procedures [ ]. VR technology, as an advanced non-pharmacological and non-invasive distraction intervention, uses head-mounted devices to create a fully immersive and interactive virtual environment for children [ ]. This approach achieves a cognitive and emotional “transfer” of the child away from the immediate medical context, reducing attention to pain signals and the brain’s perception of pain, thereby alleviating the child’s pain and anxiety [ ]. Currently, evidence-based practice internationally has gradually confirmed the positive role of VR in pediatric procedural pain management [ , ]. While international studies on this topic are abundant, they primarily focus on pediatric outpatient and emergency settings [ , , ], with relatively insufficient research on inpatient ward environments. Hospitalized children often undergo repeated medical procedures, and the psychological stress they experience is both cumulative and context-specific, warranting in-depth exploration [ ]. This perspective aligns with the broader landscape of assistive and emerging technologies designed to detect and reduce neurophysiological stress and anxiety in children [ ], further supporting the rationale for implementing VR-based interventions in hospitalized pediatric populations. A recent high-quality study [ ] demonstrated that the use of commercially available VR devices during peripheral venous catheterization in a pediatric emergency department did not yield significant positive effects. This finding suggests that the efficacy of VR-based distraction interventions may be moderated by multiple factors, including environmental urgency, the child’s baseline anxiety level, the age-appropriateness and immersiveness of VR content, and the adequacy of pre-procedural preparation. In fast-paced, high-pressure emergency settings, commercial VR devices may be insufficient to effectively capture children’s attention within limited preparation time. In contrast, the more controlled and predictable environment of inpatient wards may allow for better-tailored and more thoroughly prepared VR interventions, potentially enhancing their therapeutic effects. Therefore, to address the inconsistencies in the aforementioned findings and further explore the application value of VR in inpatient pediatric care, this study employs the Attention Resource Limitation Theory [ ] and the Gate Control Theory [ ] as its theoretical frameworks. The Attentional Resource Limitation Theory posits that an individual’s total attentional capacity is limited. When VR experience engages a significant portion of this capacity, the cognitive resources available for processing pain are consequently reduced. The Gate Control Theory explains the underlying neural mechanism, proposing that non-noxious sensory input (such as the visual and auditory stimuli provided by VR) can activate inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord’s dorsal horn. This activation effectively “closes the gate,” impeding the transmission of pain signals to the brain. Therefore, by delivering a highly immersive multi-sensory experience, the VR intervention is anticipated to competitively occupy the child’s attentional resources and engage the endogenous pain-inhibitory pathways, thereby achieving a reduction in the perception of pain and anxiety. By focusing on the stable setting of inpatient wards and comparing VR interventions with conventional care, this research aims to determine whether VR can reliably reduce pain and anxiety in hospitalized children. Additionally, this study will systematically evaluate the applicability, tolerability, and potential limitations of VR devices in hospitalized children, with the goal of providing empirical evidence and practical references for clinical practice. 2. By focusing on the stable setting of inpatient wards and comparing VR interventions with conventional care, this research aims to determine whether VR can reliably reduce pain and anxiety in hospitalized children. Additionally, this study will systematically evaluate the applicability, tolerability, and potential limitations of VR devices in hospitalized children, with the goal of providing empirical evidence and practical references for clinical practice. 2. Methods 2.1. Study Design and Participants We conducted a single-center, parallel-group, randomized controlled trial (registered on 18 December 2025, at the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry; registration number: ChiCTR2500114904). This study report adheres to the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) guidelines [ ]. This study employed convenience sampling to select pediatric patients requiring peripheral venous catheterization in the pediatric ward of Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, from July to December 2024. Inclusion criteria: (a) Hospitalized children aged 5–14 years; (b) Children with normal comprehension and communication abilities who actively participated; and (c) Voluntary participation in the trial. Exclusion criteria: (a) Children with visual or auditory impairments; (b) Children with psychiatric history, severe cardiovascular disease, or other physical illnesses; (c) Children unable to fully complete questionnaires with nursing assistance; (d) Children who had taken analgesics within the past week; and (e) Uncooperative children, defined as those who refused to follow verbal instructions during the pre-procedure preparation or expressed unwillingness to undergo the catheterization despite caregiver reassurance. Based on relevant literature [ ], S = 8.81, δ = 6.15, α = 0.05, and u α = 1.96 were selected; With β = 0.20, u β = 0.8416. Substituting these values yields n 1 = n 2 = 34 cases. Considering an approximate 15% sample attrition rate and non-response bias, the experimental and control groups each comprise 40 cases. 2.2. Randomization and Blinding This study employed simple randomization with a 1:1 allocation ratio. The randomization sequence was generated by an independent statistician using computer-generated random numbers. Allocation concealment was ensured through the use of sequentially numbered, sealed, opaque envelopes to maintain the unpredictability of the assignment process. The enrolling researcher, who was not involved in sequence generation, opened the next envelope to assign eligible participants to either the intervention group or the control group. However, due to the readily identifiable nature of the intervention (the use of VR devices), it was not feasible to blind participants, researchers, or healthcare professionals. To minimize potential bias, data analysts remained blinded to group allocation throughout the study. The unblinding plan was as follows: unblinding would occur after the completion of the study and final statistical analysis of the data; emergency unblinding would be implemented if a child experienced serious adverse events during the study. 2.3. Interventions 2.3.1. Establishment of the Research Team The research team comprised one ward nurse manager, one senior nurse practitioner, one attending physician, and one nursing graduate student. The nurse manager reviewed the VR content design and supervised implementation, while the senior nurse practitioner strictly adhered to peripheral venous catheterization standards when performing the procedure and corresponding health education for both groups of pediatric patients. The nursing graduate student monitored the heart rate of both groups of pediatric patients using a finger pulse oximeter (Yuwell YX306, manufactured by Jiangsu Yuwell Medical Equipment & Supply Co., Ltd., Jiangsu, China) during the procedure and collected data on pain, anxiety, satisfaction scores, catheterization time, and VR applicability assessment forms. The attending physician monitored the patients’ reactions during the catheterization procedure and immediately addressed any adverse reactions. Adverse events, including but not limited to dizziness, nausea, eye fatigue, and any signs of distress, were actively monitored and recorded by the attending physician and nursing graduate student for all participants throughout the procedure. The intervention was to be discontinued immediately in the event of any serious adverse event. 2.3.2. Development of Intervention Protocol Literature reviews on VR applications for pediatric peripheral venous catheterization were conducted domestically and internationally. Analysis of pain and anxiety levels during catheterization, along with corresponding physiological changes, informed the initial intervention protocol developed through repeated discussions by the research team. A pilot study was conducted with 15 eligible patients in each group (control and observation). The final intervention protocol was refined based on issues identified during the pilot study. The intervention plan details are as follows: (1) Timing: After the baseline survey, the experimental group begins VR intervention upon entering the pediatric procedure room and continues it throughout the standard care procedures until the conclusion of the catheterization procedure. (2) Implementer: The same senior nurse performed peripheral venous catheterization and health education for both groups. Family members were present but did not participate in the intervention. (3) Duration: The VR intervention for the experimental group lasted from 5 min before the catheterization procedure until its completion, with the entire process taking 10–15 min; (4) Game Video Content: Five suitable 360° video contents were selected from the PICO neo3 software store after review by the research team and added to the favorites ( ). After review and consent by the patients’ families, the research nurse assisted in playing the videos. 2.3.3. Determining Research Tools Based on the integration of research requirements, literature analysis, and market survey results, the PICO Neo3 VR all-in-one headset was ultimately selected as the intervention tool for the experimental group due to its suitability for playing virtual videos. This study utilizes a fully enclosed virtual headset that continuously captures environmental features through four wide-angle cameras mounted on the headset. Built-in speakers on both sides deliver spatial audio for enhanced immersion, while foam padding conforms to the face and adjustable straps ensure comfort for extended wear. When pediatric patients wear the VR headset to view virtual content, the three-dimensional images dynamically adjust in real-time with minor head movements. This design maintains immersion while preventing significant head swivel that could interfere with medical staff operations. 2.3.4. Implementation of Intervention Methods Intervention Group Upon entering the pediatric procedure room, children in the experimental group received routine care. A researcher then demonstrated the virtual reality equipment, explaining its operation in simple, easy-to-understand language. The researcher assisted the child in wearing the headset and invited them to try it for 5 min. After opening the PICO Store favorites interface, children of different ages and genders selected videos based on their preferences. Following the 5 min trial, the researcher notified the nurse to begin catheterization. During this procedure, the child continued using the VR headset until completion. The researcher then assisted in removing the headset, inquired about the child’s experience, and guided them through completing various assessment forms. Throughout the virtual reality experience, researchers remained present to observe the children’s reactions ( ). Control Group A senior nurse performed peripheral venous catheterization and routine care for enrolled patients. This included pre-procedure explanations to patients and families regarding the purpose of the catheterization, assessment of the insertion site, and detailed instructions on the procedure and related precautions. They covered daily catheter maintenance, preventing catheter dislodgement, fixation methods, daily life considerations, and potential catheter-related complications such as bleeding, post-removal needle site care, etc. Prior to the procedure, the nurse performing the placement encouraged and reassured the child to alleviate anxiety. Family members were also permitted to provide comfort, such as through hugs. 2.4. Measurements 2.4.1. Pain Level The primary outcome was pain, assessed using the Wong–Baker Faces Pain Rating Scale (WB-FPRS) in both groups of pediatric patients: 10 min prior to peripheral venous catheterization (T0), at the conclusion of catheterization (T1), and 30 min post-catheterization (T2). Developed by Wong et al. [ ], this scale comprises six facial expressions ranging from smiling to sadness to crying. Scores ranged from 0 to 10, representing no pain, little pain, mild pain, noticeable pain, severe pain, and intense pain, respectively. Each score level corresponded to a specific facial expression. Children selected one expression to represent their pain intensity at the time of scoring. This scale is suitable for assessing acute pain in children [ ]. 2.4.2. Anxiety Assessment Anxiety was assessed as a key secondary outcome using the Visual Analog Scale for Anxiety (VAS-A) at 10 min before peripheral venous catheterization (T0), at the completion of catheterization (T1), and 30 min after catheterization (T2). The scale ranges from 0 to 10. The leftmost score of 0 indicates no anxiety, while the rightmost score of 10 represents maximum anxiety. Children selected one expression to represent their pain intensity at the time of scoring. All children self-rated their pain independently, with the researcher providing standardized instructions. Caregiver assistance was permitted only if the child required help understanding the scale. This scale has demonstrated good reliability and validity for effectively measuring subjective anxiety [ ]. 2.4.3. Comparison of Pediatric Patients’ Heart Rate, Catheterization Duration, and Procedure Satisfaction From 10 min before peripheral venous catheterization to 30 min after its completion, heart rate and oxygen saturation were continuously monitored using a finger-clip pulse oximeter and recorded by the researchers. The data collected included heart rate 10 min before venipuncture (T0), peak heart rate during catheterization (Tmax), and heart rate 30 min after catheterization (T2). A stopwatch was used to record the time from disinfection to completion of peripheral venous catheter fixation. Patient satisfaction was assessed using a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from “completely dissatisfied” (1 point) to “very satisfied” (5 points). The satisfaction percentage (%) was calculated as (number of “very satisfied” + “somewhat satisfied” cases)/total cases × 100%. 2.4.4. Suitability of VR Goggles Factors such as the patient’s educational background, age, level of exposure to electronic devices, and tolerance for external interventions may all influence the suitability of virtual reality. To obtain authentic feedback on VR interventions, our research team conducted a systematic review of relevant literature and based on observations from prior trials, refined five questions through group discussions to facilitate a basic assessment of virtual reality’s suitability. 2.5. Data Collection Prior to intervention, both groups of pediatric patients were required to provide basic information such as age and diagnosis for assessment. We provided paper-based questionnaires to the patients, which took approximately 10 min to complete. If caregivers could not recall specific medical history details, they could leave those sections blank; we would later retrieve necessary information from the medical record system. To minimize bias in outcome assessment, all subjective scale administrations were conducted by a dedicated outcome assessor who was not involved in VR delivery. The assessor used standardized, scripted instructions for each scale to ensure consistency across participants and groups. The assessor remained blinded to group allocation whenever feasible, although complete blinding was limited by the observable nature of VR use. Peripheral venous catheterization procedures and health education for both groups were performed by the same senior nurse. Physiological data and procedure duration were recorded by the outcome assessor using standardized forms. All data were double-checked and entered to ensure completeness and accuracy. 2.6. Data Analysis In formal studies, data were entered and verified by two individuals before statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 27.0 software. Quantitative data were first assessed for normality through the Shapiro–Wilk test. Quantitative data conforming to normal distribution were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (mean ± SD), with intergroup comparisons performed using the independent samples t -test. Non-normally distributed quantitative data were expressed as median (25th percentile, 75th percentile), i.e., M ( P 25 , P 75 ), with intergroup comparisons using the Mann–Whitney U test. Categorical data were compared between groups using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact probability method. Pain and anxiety scores at different intervention time points were analyzed using Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE), with grouping, time points, and the interaction between grouping and time points serving as explanatory variables. For the GEE models, a Gaussian distribution with an identity link function was assumed for both pain and anxiety scores, given their approximately continuous nature. An unstructured working correlation matrix was specified to account for within-subject correlations across time points without imposing a predefined pattern. Robust standard errors were used to obtain valid inference even if the working correlation structure was misspecified. No missing data occurred for pain or anxiety outcomes at any time point, as all participants completed all assessments. For normally distributed data, Cohen’s d was used to estimate the effect of the VR intervention, while for skewed data, the Rank-biserial r effect size was employed. Discussion Main findings: Postprocedural reports indicated that VR reduced pain scores and was associated with lower overall anxiety scores in children receiving peripheral intravenous catheterization ( p < 0.05). This finding is consistent with the conclusions of most previous studies [ , , ], further confirming the positive role of VR intervention in alleviating procedural pain and anxiety in pediatric patients. GEE analysis further revealed that the mechanisms by which VR affects pain and anxiety differ ( and ). A significant time-by-group interaction effect was observed for pain scores (β = 0.775, Wald χ 2 = 5.897, p = 0.015), indicating that VR alters the trajectory of pain over time. In contrast, no significant interaction effect was found for anxiety scores (β = 0.250, Wald χ 2 = 0.148, p = 0.700), indicating that the reduction in anxiety over time followed a similar pattern in both groups, and VR did not significantly alter the trajectory of anxiety. This distinction is crucial: while VR effectively buffers the immediate pain experience by modifying its temporal course, its impact on anxiety appears to operate through a main effect—lowering overall levels—rather than by changing the natural decline of anxiety over time. From a theoretical perspective, these findings provide empirical support for the Gate Control Theory and the Attention Resource Limitation Theory. According to Gate Control Theory [ ], VR provides rich visual and auditory stimuli that activate large-diameter nerve fibers, effectively “closing the gate” on pain signal transmission at the spinal cord level. The significant between-group differences and interaction effects observed in pain scores corroborate this mechanism. VR, as a “top-down” cognitive intervention, indeed alters the pain perception process [ ]. The absence of an interaction effect for anxiety can be explained by Attention Resource Limitation Theory [ ]: children have limited cognitive resources. Although VR can reduce absolute anxiety levels by occupying attention, it cannot override the inherent tendency for anxiety to naturally subside over time, which explains why the trajectory of anxiety reduction did not differ between groups. In other words, VR has a more direct effect on acute pain, whereas its effect on anticipatory and cognitively constructed emotional anxiety is largely superimposed upon the natural recovery process. However, compared to the negative findings of Samina Ali et al. [ ] conducted in an emergency department setting, the positive results of this study may benefit from environmental advantages. Attention Resource Limitation Theory posits that a stable environment minimizes competition for cognitive resources from external stimuli, allowing VR to achieve attentional dominance. In this study, the intervention was conducted in a quiet, dedicated preparation room, providing children sufficient time to familiarize themselves with the equipment and engage with the virtual scenario—conditions conducive to VR’s effectiveness. In contrast, the chaotic and unpredictable environment of the emergency department continuously distracts children’s attention, preventing VR from effectively occupying their cognitive resources and thereby diluting the intervention effects [ ]. This suggests that the clinical efficacy of VR results from the interaction between theoretical mechanisms and environmental conditions. Pain, as a multidimensional experience, directly triggers physiological stress responses, such as changes in heart rate and blood oxygen saturation [ , ]. This study observed that the maximum heart rate of children in the VR intervention group during catheterization was significantly lower than that of the control group ( p < 0.05). This finding not only aligns with the report by Eda Orhan et al. [ ] but may also reveal the physiological benefits of VR intervention from a deeper level. The reduction in heart rate may not be solely attributed to diminished pain perception; it may signify a mitigation of the overall stress response system. When VR successfully diverts attention, the overactivation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis may be suppressed, leading to a decrease in sympathetic nervous system excitability, which manifests as stabilized heart rate. This improvement in physiological state, combined with the alleviation of psychological anxiety, works synergistically to create better conditions for subsequent procedures [ ]. [ ]. The reduction in procedure time is directly attributable to the children’s higher cooperation and reduced resistance due to decreased pain and anxiety. Behind this, there may also be a more subtle interactive mechanism: when the children are calmer, the urgency and confrontational pressure faced by the operating nurses are also reduced, potentially allowing them to perform the procedure more calmly and precisely, thereby indirectly improving operational efficiency. This virtuous cycle of positive interaction between healthcare providers and patients not only enhances the efficiency and experience of a single procedure but also holds profound long-term significance for improving doctor-patient relationships, reducing medical fear, and enhancing children’s future compliance with medical care. In terms of applicability assessment, the VR goggles demonstrated good clinical suitability in this study, which is consistent with the conclusions of Tychsen et al. [ ]. Minor eye fatigue reported by a few children may be related to visual stimulation parameters of the video content, such as color saturation, contrast, or dynamic frequency. A systematic review [ ] on the safety of virtual reality technology use in children under 14 years of age indicated that VR may cause mild cybersickness, and for children with amblyopia, VR use may lead to diplopia. Therefore, it is recommended to conduct a pre-assessment of the safety and suitability for pediatric patients before implementing VR intervention. The high level of interest in VR content (90% found it effective, 95% willing to use it again) demonstrates its exceptional appeal and acceptability. However, individual cases also exposed the limitations of existing devices: one child was indifferent to using VR goggles because anxiety about potential pain during treatment prevented full immersion in the game state; another child refused because not being able to see the surrounding environment made them feel more afraid; one child rated the goggles as relatively uncomfortable because they tended to slip during the procedure, affecting video viewing. This sharply highlights that current VR devices are primarily designed for adults and do not adequately consider the diverse needs of pediatric patients in terms of ergonomics (e.g., head circumference, nose bridge fit) and experience modes (e.g., whether environmental transparency is provided). Therefore, developing or adapting pediatric-specific devices suitable for different age groups and capable of flexibly adjusting immersion levels (e.g., mixed reality modes) is a key direction for future technological translation. In summary, VR technology, through multi-dimensional mechanisms of attention capture and diversion, can effectively alleviate pain and anxiety during venous catheterization in hospitalized children in suitable environments, leading to a chain of benefits such as physiological improvement and increased operational efficiency. Due to technological revolutions and competitive marketing, VR has become more convenient and widely accessible [ ]. VR is a fixed asset, as a single set of VR equipment can be reused multiple times across multiple patients. Additionally, VR hardware is easy to store and maintain. By replacing variable costs with fixed costs, virtual reality has profound implications for reducing healthcare costs [ ]. It is recommended that this technology be systematically promoted and applied in pediatric inpatient wards, provided that environmental suitability is fully considered. 5. Limitations Due to the inherent characteristics of VR technology, blinding of nurses and researchers was not feasible in this study, which represents a methodological limitation. The relatively narrow score range of the scale used in this study resulted in a floor effect at baseline (T0): the median pain score was 0 in both groups, the median anxiety score was 5 in both groups, and within-group variability was limited. This floor effect for pain scores at baseline is consistent with the fact that children had not yet undergone the painful procedure at the time of measurement, leaving little room for downward change in pain scores over time. Consequently, this baseline clustering phenomenon reduced the sensitivity to detect intervention effects—even if the VR intervention was truly effective, statistically significant differences would be difficult to detect. Therefore, when interpreting the between-group differences observed in this study, this limitation inherent to the measurement tool must be considered. Adverse events were actively monitored

In addition, the VR intervention condition involved a 5 min familiarization period, individualized content selection, and continuous presence of a researcher during the procedure, which constituted additional attention and interaction beyond what the control group received. This non-specific attention effect may have contributed to the observed reductions in anxiety and pain independently of the immersive VR experience itself, and this possibility should be considered when interpreting the findings. Future studies should consider enrolling populations with more pronounced baseline symptoms or adopting scales with higher sensitivity and wider score ranges to validate the intervention effects. Additionally, subjective scales may be subject to reporting bias. Additionally, there are several other shortcomings in the research: all participants were recruited from a single ward, and the limited sample size may affect the stability of the results, meaning that conclusions should be interpreted with caution when generalizing. The subjective scales used in the study may be influenced by reporting bias. Meanwhile, while the standardized VR device models and video content helped control experimental conditions, they may also restrict the applicability of the findings across different devices or intervention contents. Furthermore, as no long-term follow-up was conducted, the sustained effects of VR intervention remain unclear. Future research should involve multicenter, large-sample randomized controlled trials, incorporate diverse technical conditions and intervention protocols, and integrate objective measures with long-term follow-up to further validate the effectiveness and practical application value of VR technology. 6. Conclusions In this RCT of VR intervention for hospitalized children undergoing peripheral venous catheterization, significant improvements were observed in pain, procedure duration, and patient satisfaction with the nursing procedure following VR intervention, and overall anxiety scores were lower in the VR group, although the trajectory of anxiety reduction did not differ significantly between groups. Results also indicated that virtual reality technology demonstrated good tolerability among pediatric patients, with high willingness to use it. Given that VR is becoming increasingly affordable and accessible, it holds promise for alleviating pain and anxiety associated with peripheral venous catheterization during pediatric hospitalization, thereby significantly enhancing the healthcare experience for pediatric patients.
